articles.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
articles.description: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

articles.title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams
articles.description: The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing. There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a diaspora talking about their parents. There are refugees en masse, shorn of any traits or qualities at all, discussed purely in terms of whether or not the host state can accommodate them, and how long they should be a

articles.title: The hill I will die on: There is only one acceptable occasion on which to ghost someone – when you die | Temi Wilkey
articles.description: Dystopian dating on apps is more Thatcherite horror story than love story. Romance that blossoms through community and human connection needs a renaissance Digitising our dating lives has conditioned us all away from human connection. I spend weeks of my life huffing and puffing to keep the balloon of flirty banter in the air – with a stranger I only find vaguely attractive. I go on dates with people who are “my type on paper” but upon meeting, find the paper much better than the person. I meet a woman with a devastating mouth and an even more devastating wit, only for her to ghost . The only acceptable reason to ghost someone is if you have, in fact, died. Long ago, when Margaret Thatcher proclaimed “There is no such thing as society”, she wasn’t heralding an era of Tory rule that destroyed all public services that kept true community alive. No – she was prophesying 40 years into the future about the digital-age phenomenon of ghosting. The fact that this practice is widespread enough for there to be a word for it is proof of the long since disintegrated fabric of our society. Temi Wilkey is a writer, performer and star of the one-woman shows Main Character Energy and Lover Girl ,

articles.title: Not ready for the cold and dark? Maybe you need a ‘winter transition week’ | Emma Beddington
articles.description: A psychologist has recommended we all take time for slowness and rest, to prepare ourselves for the coming months. It’s a nice idea, but it may prove my downfall How are you feeling about the rapid dying of the light? Are you already sluggish and glum, poleaxed by the “polar vortex” or seasonal lurgy? That might be because you’re doing winter wrong: according to health psychologist Kari Leibowitz, writing in the Washington Post , we’d all benefit from a “winter transition week”. Leibowitz, the author of a book, How to Winter , based on her time living in the Arctic, explains: “I intentionally clear out my calendar … say no to extra obligations, try to cancel or postpone unnecessary meetings and make time for rest and slowness.” During this time, she also recommends stocking up on tea, getting out thick socks, eating soup and planning little treats. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial
articles.description: Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “ welcome back ” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “ Breturn ” has yet to catch on. By Friday, the mood music will be louder still. A long-awaited reset summit is due to deliver the first fruits of Mr Burnham’s ongoing rapprochement with Brussels, in the form of new deals on food and drink, and emissions trading. A symbolically powerful youth exchange agreement is also in the works, although not yet over the line. But as they promote such adjustments to existing Brexit arrangements, the prime minister’s allies have been notably keen to

articles.title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial
articles.description: From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “ war minus the shooting ”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales magnificent in beating the All Blacks on Saturday? Even those who don’t understand the finer points of the rolling maul can surely grasp why this result matters. For much of the last century, heavy industry and rugby were twin pillars of Welsh national identity. The heavy industry is largely gone, and over the past few years, rugby has looked to be going the same way: a weakened national team; financial problems that threatened to tear apart th

articles.title: Damaging the lifeline that Samaritans offers the public | Letters
articles.description: Volunteers despair as the charity sets about closing local branches and restructuring Samaritans old and new will, I’m sure, have been just as shocked as I was by your article ( ‘Is anyone up for a fight?’: The battle for the soul of Samaritans, 10 November ). Many, though, will not be surprised. I was a volunteer for 26 years in three branches. The work was demanding and life-changing; the experience is so transformative that it gives every part of society people who are strong enough to bear others’ burdens and able to share their pain. We don’t stop being listeners when we stop being volunteers. During my time, I found that the people at the top were detached from what went on at branch level. It is not news to me that they cannot understand how central to the work each local branch is and how important every human contact is to those who need to talk. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why Alan Milburn’s Pip plan is a mistake | Letters
articles.description: Savitri Hensman says financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest Alan Milburn has a track record of so-called cost-cutting measures that waste billions of pounds in public money while making health worse. The private finance initiative was an expensive mess , though it did help huge companies and rich people get richer. It is less surprising that he wants more benefits for young sick and disabled people slashed than that the government might go along with this ( Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund, 12 November ). Financially struggling families and communities will be hit the hardest. The high number of young people not in education, employment or training is probably largely due to past top-level decisions. Austerity, making life tougher for claimants while favouring multimillionaires, fewer youth clubs, underfunded mental health care, long delays in providing assessments and equipment, and making school and university more stressful have not only caused suffering but also been expensive. Continue reading...

articles.title: A fair deal on fees for EU and UK students | Letters
articles.description: Thomas Altebaeumer notes that under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, as EU students studying in the UK would Vicky Wolmuth is angered that the UK government is able to find £450m to subsidise UK universities for admitting EU students while UK students are struggling with student debt ( Letters, 10 November ). She appears to have missed that, under the proposed scheme, UK students in Europe would pay domestic fees, just as EU students studying in the UK would. Fees in the UK are among the highest in Europe. This is a political choice. Continue reading...

articles.title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
articles.description: Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes You report ( 11 November ) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock. It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle. Continue reading...

articles.title: Will Joseph poised to start for England against All Blacks after five-try burst

articles.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?
articles.description: Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The Saudi-backed government explained the repositioning by saying the strategic priority was to break the attritional siege on Taiz , Yemen’s third city, and to protect Aden, the southern port city in which the Saudi-backed and UN-recognised government is now based. Continue reading...

Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her first trial ended in a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was criminally responsible for the killings. The confirmation of Thursday’s trilateral talks, the first of their kind, will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and cement Xi’s status as a global powerbroker as he presides over events in the glittering southern tech hub of Shenzhen. articles.title: Filipiñana review – sexual exploitation at the golf club in menacing satire on class and privilege
articles.description: A sense of threat permeates a verdant private golf course in water-deprived Manila, peopled with submissive tee-girls and geisha-style caddies catering to the male clientele A spectacle filled with dreamlike tableaux, off-centre framing and slow trance-like zooms, Filipiñana is an elegant and politically pointed feature debut from the Filipino director and London Film School graduate Rafael Manuel, developed from his award-winning short film of the same name. It is a melancholy satire on caste shame, sexual politics and land exploitation in the Philippines, symbolised by a private golf course in Manila, an artificial landscape as depthless and surreal as the gardens in Last Year in Marienbad . Irrigating the vivid greens and undulating fairways requires oceans of precious water – water that, in the course of one unbearable heatwave, is rationed for the sweating lower orders in the city, way beyond the golf club’s luxurious precincts. Jorrybell Agoto plays the “Filipiñana” of the title, 17-year-old Isabel, the inscrutable witness to the club’s occult traditions and one of its legion of demurely submissive uniformed “tee-girls”, whose sole purpose is to position the balls for the wea

articles.title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian
articles.description: Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14. So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapters now and again, recounting our hero’s comically tetchy exchanges with Charles. Here, really, is a sweet coming-of-age story with a delicate frosting of It’s a Wonderful Life. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy
articles.description: Filipino-US journalist Maria Ressa’s new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy – and how we can fight back Maria Ressa keeps apologising. “Sorry, I’m hyper, too much coffee!” she says at one point. “Sorry, I can rant for a long time, so you have to stop me!” she says at another. Ressa can be forgiven for firing on all cylinders. The Nobel peace prize laureate has just been to a screening in Britain of The Social Reckoning, which offers an unflattering portrayal of the tech titan Mark Zuckerberg, a man she regards as a “dictator”. Now she is speaking to the Guardian at a hotel in Washington’s Dupont Circle a few days before Americans vote in critical midterm elections. Continue reading...

articles.title: Quel head trip! Failed postcards, scrapping poets and germ-ridden film rock Paris Photo – review
articles.description: Grand Palais, Paris The fair celebrated the bicentenary of photography – but did anyone care? Especially when the most compelling images proposed whole new ways of seeing No one at the three-day Paris Photo fair seemed worried about being a target for protesters – the fate of fellow art fair Art Basel Paris, which closed two days early. “Photography isn’t expensive enough,” joked one gallerist. This 29th edition coincided with celebrations across France of the bicentenary of photography, and as such looked back at photography’s origins and the questions that have preoccupied photographers from the beginning. One example was a 19th-century portrait that is thought to be an extremely rare depiction of Rimbaud with a black eye – the poet was a known ruffian who often got physical over literary squabbles. Whether the photograph is really Rimbaud or not begs the question: what matters more, the truth, or what we believe the truth to be? After 200 years, photography hasn’t resolved the issue. The strongest thread running through Paris Photo is the uncertainty and instability of photography: as evidence that collapses into fiction and performance. Continue reading...

articles.title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways
articles.description: Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force? I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet . 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton . 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express . Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an emotional wreck? That’s what happened when I first saw director Luke Sheppard’s souped-up London revival – and again this month, watching a new film of that production. Continue reading...

articles.title: From pyjama parades to blind biscuit taste tests: how we made our ultimate festive gift guide
articles.description: We spent months putting hundreds of presents to the test – here is how we whittled them down • The best Christmas gifts for 2026 If you struggle with the idea of Christmas creep – when the festive season appears to start earlier every year – spare a thought for the team here at Filter HQ. We’ve been in Christmas mode since we packed away last year’s decorations, testing hundreds of presents for our magnum opus: the big 2026 Christmas gift guide . All 369 (we did say it was big) gifts on this year’s list were put through their paces by a crack team of testers covering all ages and tastes. Fashion writer and stylist Sam Deaman – who tested men’s accessories and nightwear – says his partner got fed up with him parading “yet another” pair of pyjamas around their bedroom each night: “It was like Stars in Their Eyes for Christmas gifts,” he says. “‘Tonight, Matthew, I’m going to be … Ebenezer Scrooge!’” Continue reading...

articles.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts
articles.description: Reared on a puppy farm, and abandoned by a previous owner, he was half-starved when we adopted him. But he grew strong, chomping through everything from dog beds to sunglasses and my debut book The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes. No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. Socks, shoes, trainers, gloves, flat caps, berets, the freshly printed chapters of my debut book, a nifty pair of 70s sunglasses. Fearless and lithe, he grabbed things we naively thought were out of reach, and woe betide anyone who tried to take them from him. Continue reading...

articles.title: A job that changed me: Washing hands at a luxury skincare brand, I learned how fascism could feel ‘aesthetic’
articles.description: The brand had cherrypicked fragments of the Futurist Manifesto for decoration – as if they referred to a hydrating night mask, rather than a violent new world order Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email In a group interview for a luxury skincare brand – the one everyone jokes is a cult – a tall woman in a sack dress told us they preferred to hire people without any previous experience in skincare. “We find they need to un learn a lot of what they think they know.” I was 19, happy to kneel on the converted warehouse’s concrete floor to demonstrate my enthusiasm for teamwork, building a structure from drinking straws with other retail candidates. And, when I got it, that job was my gateway to Melbourne. I’d just moved and suddenly my life was brimming with cool and clever people, recommendations for art, music and food, and a dizzying number of expensive skincare products, stashed haphazardly in my share house bathroom. The perks were delightful. I paid rent with Centrelink and applied $200 face gel for my hangovers. Sign up for our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morning Continue reading...

articles.title: Jess Elliott Dennison’s quick and easy recipe for ricotta dumplings with sage butter, rocket and lemon | Quick and easy
articles.description: Easy cheesy dumplings with the perfect level of lightness and squidge Making gnocchi from scratch can be a bit of a faff midweek. However, these ricotta-and-parmesan-based dumplings are so easy to throw together, and always come out light and with just the right amount of squidge. Sage and brown butter feels the right sauce at this time of year, but you could serve them with a simple tomato sauce instead. Any leftover dumplings work a treat thrown into a brothy, minestrone-type soup. Continue reading...

articles.title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating
articles.description: I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living. During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism. Continue reading...

articles.title: Road Improvement Scheme York Street 18 Sept - 16 Oct

The carriageway resurfacing scheme will extend for a distance of 800 metres from the Brougham Street junction to just beyond the junction of the Limestone Road. To facilitate the scheme, it will be necessary to implement road closures over four consecutive weekends. From 9.00pm on Friday 2 October 2026 until 6.00pm on Sunday 4 October 2026. From 6.00am on Saturday 10 October 2026 until 6.00pm on Sunday 11 October 2026. articles.title: NI Water Works - Cornagrade Road Enniskillen 3 Aug
articles.description: Essential Water Infrastructure Improvement Work gets underway – Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen NI Water is set to commence an upgrade of the water infrastructure on Cornagrade Road, Enniskillen in early August for approximately 6 weeks. The work will see around 400m of new watermain being laid along Cornagrade Road, starting at Cherrymount Roundabout on Monday 3 rd August and progressing as far as the second entrance to Kilmacormick Road. To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. Working areas will be kept as short as possible (around 100m) with temporary traffic lights in place to manage the flow of traffic. Access to residential and business properties on and adjacent to Cornagrade Road will be available at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be affected for a short period of time while the pipelaying passes. Any bus stop located within a working area will be temporarily relocated.

articles.title: Derry - NIW Scheme - Racecourse Rd - from 27 July
articles.description: Essential water network upgrade to get underway on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett NI Water is set to begin an essential watermain upgrade on Racecourse Road, Ballyarnett (Derry/Londonderry) on Monday 27 th July to improve the resilience of the local water supply network. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.description: The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is staring down the barrel of entering 2027 without a chair for the first time in its 51-year history. Unable to win over Ankara, Europe should drop its objections to Tbilisi to avert a crisis. With three weeks to go until the OSCE Ministerial Council in Lugano, Switzerland, on December 3, the organization remains deadlocked over who should lead it from 2027-28. The chairperson-in-office role rotates every two years and is normally voted on well in advance with agreement by consensus. articles.title: Nvidia Lacks Corporate D&O Insurance Amid Huang Scandal
articles.description: Nvidia Lacks Corporate D&O Insurance Amid Huang Scandal Nvidia does not have directors’ and officers’ (D&O) liability insurance covering the company itself, an unusual omission for a major US-listed corporation that could leave the chipmaker facing substantial legal costs amid the controversy surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang, according to Financial Times . The FT writes that while Nvidia reportedly maintains $900mn in insurance protecting its directors and senior executives from personal liability, the policy does not extend to the company’s own financial exposure. The coverage, arranged through Aon and involving insurers including Beazley, AIG and Chubb, is limited to what the industry calls Side A protection. Most large publicly traded US companies also purchase Side B and Side C insurance, which can reimburse corporate legal expenses and cover certain claims brought directly against the company. Nvidia’s decision to operate without these protections is uncommon, although high premiums can lead some businesses to retain such risks themselves. Yet, the most enduring and permanent legacy of Washington's endless wars is rarely debated or discussed: mass demographic engineering . For decades, the foreign policy of the United States has operated as a relentless engine of human displacement. articles.description: The Death Of Real Life: We've Confused Technological Progress With Human Progress Authored by Spyridon Andrews via American Greatness , I hate the digital age. There, I've said it. Go ahead, call me whatever you want. I'm a Luddite, an unenlightened Boomer, a dinosaur, or whatever other insult comes to mind. I don't really care. In fact, if Boomers didn't care what their parents thought, we certainly don't care what our kids think. Although I suspect that, having lived long enough to see how things have turned out, more than a few of us regret not listening to our parents a little more carefully. But that's a story for another day. I've lived in the previous world, and I've lived in this one, and I'm not particularly impressed with this one. We've traded much of what makes us human for the ability to do things faster, more conveniently, and with as little human interaction as possible. We've confused technological progress with human progress, and I suspect that when we finally look back on all of this, we'll conclude that we made a terrible bargain. The world I grew up in is gone. articles.description: "Hawks Flying In Formation": Judge Refuses To Toss DRAM Cartel Suit Against Samsung, SK Hynix And Micron, Opening Door To Discovery For the past year, the only people with the power to do anything about memory prices have been the three companies that set them. As of this weekend, a federal judge in San Jose has joined the list. Regular readers know we have spent most of 2026 chronicling what soaring memory prices have done to everything they touch: PC shipments in January, producer prices in June, Apple's price list shortly after, and by July the Fed itself, when we reported that Goldman saw AI-driven memory, software and electricity costs adding 0.5% to core PCE by year-end . Well, year-end is six weeks away, memory prices are still in orbit, and the question of why supply never showed up is now officially a matter for discovery. In an order dated Nov. 14, Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied in full the joint motion by Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron (MU) to dismiss the proposed class action accusing the three of conspiring to choke off the supply of conventional DRAM. articles.title: Tell us: did you move to the countryside for retirement and come to regret it?
articles.description: As England’s chief medical officer warns of the challenges of growing older in rural areas, we’d like to hear from people who have struggled with isolation or accessing services and support England’s chief medical officer Chris Whitty has warned of the potential downsides of choosing to spend the later part of your life in a rural area. He urged people to think carefully about the challenges of rural life as they get older, including poor access to healthcare, limited public transport and the risk of becoming isolated or dependent on others. We want to hear from the people people who have experienced these challenges. Did you move to the countryside for your retirement and find it more difficult to access the services and support you need? Are you feeling dependent on others to get around and access amenities, leaving you wishing you’d stayed in a town or city? Or have you moved back to a city, finding rural life too isolating as you become older? Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I found the best mountain view in Europe’: readers’ favourite wild escapes in Scotland
articles.description: From the Isle of Skye to the Cairngorms, our explorers find white-sand beaches, secret lochs and solitude • Tell us about your favourite European national park – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher At Camasunary bay on the Strathaird peninsula of the Isle of Skye, we watched an otter at low tide lifting seaweed to find crabs. Boots off, we crossed one of Skye’s shortest (and coldest) rivers, before slogging upwards through unforgiving heather to the col beneath the pathless hill Sgùrr na Strì . The mountain view from the summit’s glaciated slabs is perhaps the finest in Scotland – or even Europe. Below is landlocked Loch Coruisk, girdled by the black teeth of the entire Cuillin ridge. Extraordinary. An hour passed, maybe two, before we headed back. The otter was by then long gone, hopefully just as replete and satisfied as we were. Hugh Jones Continue reading...

articles.title: Tim Dowling: I’ve made being ill an art form – and my wife has notes
articles.description: I’m so tired of this illness, I wonder if an acting-led approach to faking wellness might help me recover It is late morning on a Wednesday, and I’m sitting at the kitchen table collapsing in on myself, because I am ill. I feel dizzy, and feverish, and achy, and I have done for two days. I’m gently resting my damp forehead on the table when my wife walks in. “Ugh,” I say. Continue reading...

articles.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
articles.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

articles.title: Microsoft outage: company scrambles to fix global issue that took down Outlook and Teams
articles.description: Tech firm says it is ‘deeply sorry’ for disruption that took services down and has now addressed the underlying issue What caused the outage and when will it be fixed? Microsoft outage hits UK hospitals, GPs, schools and police Tell us: have you been affected by the outage? Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”. The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘So lovely’: Stevie Wonder surprises Stalybridge restaurant with late-night visit and £1,000 tip
articles.description: Singer, 76, was in Manchester with his band for penultimate UK show of his Songs in the Key of Life anniversary tour When Stevie Wonder’s team just called to say: “Can we all come to your restaurant in Stalybridge at 11pm on a Sunday?” Ryan Robinson, of course, said yes. First the band turned up, and then – at 12.30am – the man himself arrived. Hours later, staff at the Cafe Continental were sharing a £1,000 tip. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best electric toothbrushes in the UK for every budget
articles.description: We put 32 electric toothbrushes to the test, from oscillating Oral-B models to sustainable brands like Suri, to find the best for cleaning power and value for money • How to make your toothbrush last longer If you grew up using a conventional toothbrush – essentially a stick with bristles on the end – you may be surprised to learn just how long the electric toothbrush has been around. The first was designed in the late 1930s, but that model was a long way from the sleek, feature-packed and Bluetooth-enabled beasts you can buy today. There are now dozens of ultra-advanced versions on the market, but which ones are worth your cash? To help answer that question, my teeth have become figurative guinea pigs. Over the past two years, I’ve put 32 electric toothbrushes from the likes of Dyson, Oral-B, Philips, Suri, Ordo, Silk’n and Foreo through their paces to separate the best from the rest. Here are my conclusions. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: One of Britain’s oldest surviving traditions – and it’s all over in four minutes | Doc Rowe
articles.description: Ryton-on-Dunsmore, Warwickshire: It takes place in the dark, and this year there’s misty rain to contend with, but the wroth silver ceremony has endured for centuries Before sunrise on 11 November, while most people are still sleeping, representatives of 25 Warwickshire parishes gather on Knightlow Hill to observe one of Britain’s oldest surviving customs. The wroth silver ceremony is at least 850 years old, first appearing in written records in 1170, and requires payment of annual rent to the landowner, the Duke of Buccleuch. Despite misty rain this year, more than 60 people attend amid the noise of traffic from the A45. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
articles.description: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing? T he romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time. Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”. Continue reading...

articles.title: Immersive show brings Kyffin Williams’ rugged Welsh landscapes to life
articles.description: Paintings by one of country’s most important artists have been animated and set to music at National Library of Wales The paintings of artists such as Vincent van Gogh, Paul Cézanne and David Hockney have been brought to life in all-singing, all-dancing immersive shows in recent years. Now one of Wales’s most important artists, Sir Kyffin Williams , known for capturing the spectacular landscapes of his homeland with layers of paint thickly applied with a palette knife, has been given the same treatment. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Don’t lie to me to get free stuff’: how small businesses are fighting back against influencers
articles.description: From diva-like behaviour to freebie requests that never result in a review, ‘entitled’ content creators are a growing blight on small-business owners. Now entrepreneurs are calling them out Nicole Flanagin remembers exactly the moment an influencer came after her business. It was the early hours of a March morning and the cat cafe owner in Lenoir, North Carolina, got a message. “At 1.37,” she says, “a friend sent me the link to this girl’s TikTok.” The 41-year-old was already having a bad 24 hours. A mother of four, Flanagin also works at a pet rescue shelter and had spent the previous day unsuccessfully fighting for a dog not to be put down. She got home exhausted and promptly conked out in bed. Then she woke up to the message. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s an architect’s dream’: five beautiful eco buildings around the world
articles.description: From a bamboo gym in Bali to a house made from earth in Wiltshire, these projects show the beauty in sustainable design With construction accounting for more than a third of global emissions, sustainable architecture is central to the world meeting its climate targets. The following five creations from around the world exemplify how “green” buildings can also be beautiful. Children’s Village, Tocantins, Brazil Continue reading...

articles.title: Philippines’ Carmelle wins first Eurovision contest in Asia
articles.description: Filipino entry, pop and rap song Sobra-Sobra, takes 19-year-old to victory at grand final in Bangkok Carmelle Collado has won the first Eurovision song contest Asia, taking the Philippines’ entry, Sobra-Sobra , to victory in Bangkok on Saturday night, at the first regional edition of the contest to be staged outside Europe. Eleven countries competed at the One Bangkok Forum in central Bangkok, and the show ran for two and a half hours including advertising. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
articles.description: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...

articles.title: Britain’s veto could stop the UAE’s choice from running the United Nations. Miliband must use it | Steve Bloomfield
articles.description: Lana Nusseibeh appears to have the support of Russia and the US, but her role glossing the horror in Sudan makes her unsuitable – and we should say so Since the devastating war in Sudan began in 2023, some of the best investigative work uncovering those responsible has been carried out by the UN panel of experts. Its reports have revealed clear evidence that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has been funnelling weapons and providing mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide . It is these reports, produced by UN-funded investigators, that the UN secretary general, António Guterres, cites whenever he speaks about Sudan. Continue reading...

articles.title: Looking for an ancient tree worth a detour? There’s an app for that
articles.description: Dutch designer sets up an app to help fellow enthusiasts find the great trees of the world While most people spend their holidays sightseeing or lazing by a pool, Hidde Burgmans would rather seek out special trees. While not an expert in the subject, the 37-year-old from Baarn in the Netherlands has developed what he cheerfully admits is something of an obsession. He even managed to propose to his girlfriend, Nadia Roeleveld, under a particularly special cedar in Japan: “My fiancee always laughs, because she’s like, ‘OK, we have to make a detour again because Hidde found another big tree’.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
articles.description: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. Ebony Riddell Bamber is the programme director of the Scott Trust’s Legacies of Enslavement progr

articles.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
articles.description: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

articles.title: Is Burnham’s plan for a housing revolution anything more than a pipedream? | John Harris
articles.description: Nearly 2 million children are housed in dire conditions, anxious families are living out of carrier bags. There’s little sign of the hope our PM promised Two days after the Christmas of 2024, Andy Burnham put up a post on X that linked to a piece about housing in the Guardian. The then mayor of Greater Manchester, who was beginning to find his voice as a frank critic of Keir Starmer’s new government, did not mess about: “The Government should make building hundreds of thousands of council homes its defining purpose,” he said. “No other policy, achievable within a parliament, would have greater social and economic benefits.” In his first Labour conference speech as party leader and prime minister, Burnham reprised much the same argument, promising “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar era”. But by that point, he had also served notice that his commitment to a thoroughgoing council house revival might not be quite as cast iron as it seemed. The previous month, having insisted that all of the £39bn Rachel Reeves had promised to spend on the Starmer government’s Social and Affordable Homes Programme (SAHP) until 2036 should go on homes for social rent, he made

articles.title: ‘If you don’t shower, so what?’ The western diplomats staying put in under-attack Kyiv
articles.description: Ambassadors say presence sends powerful signal of solidarity and support amid escalation in Russian strikes and warnings The warning from Moscow was blunt. Western diplomats should immediately leave the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv . If they failed to do so they would be “in mortal danger”. The statement added that Russia would not be responsible for any “potential negative consequences” if its advice was ignored. European envoys in Kyiv responded to the Kremlin’s threat last month with a loud raspberry. Denmark’s ambassador to Ukraine, Thomas Lund-Sørensen, took to social media to say that he was staying . So did the ambassadors from Germany, Italy, Spain, Sweden, France, Poland and Estonia . Even the Americans indicated they would not be budging. Continue reading...

articles.title: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
articles.description: Prime minister promises ‘root-and-branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits Andy Burnham: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Continue reading...

articles.title: Obama portrait artist draws Burnham for Big Issue cover to highlight rough sleeping vow
articles.description: Exclusive: Shepard Fairey says image will hold PM accountable over promise to get people off the streets The “Hope” portrait of Barack Obama by the US street artist Shepard Fairey came to symbolise a historic 2008 presidential campaign, became one of the most ubiquitous and reproduced political portraits of modern times, and ended up in the Smithsonian. Fairey’s latest work, of the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, may not elicit the same response but will, he hopes, deliver a hard-hitting message: one of a promise made. Continue reading...

articles.title: The crisis facing Britain’s young people is politicians’ fault. To fix it, we need a generational response | Andy Burnham
articles.description: Alan Milburn’s review will mark a watershed moment for our approach to welfare and childhood. This is how I’m determined to create change Report: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis A generation of young people did not wake up one morning and decide they did not want to work. The fact that a million 16- to 24-year-olds are now not in education, employment or training (Neet) is not their fault. It is ours, as politicians. We have failed to give them the support they need as they have grown up in a tougher world. This has become an economic catastrophe for the country – and a moral one too. Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom Continue reading...

articles.title: When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price
articles.description: Fallout from ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair is the latest reminder of the shared toll paid when patriarchs cheat From Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart , Bill Gates and Bill Clinton , history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang. These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well … Continue reading...

articles.title: Why would anyone want a smart fridge? | Dave Schilling
articles.description: After a hack in France, internet-enabled appliances are looking even less appealing – especially before the holidays We are deep into the holiday season now, past Halloween and a mere two weeks away from American Thanksgiving. I’ve already given up taking care of my body, surrendering fully to gluttony, vices, and going to bed at 7pm because it’s pitch black outside. I’ve begun to hibernate like a slothful bear, my blanket and pillow never too far from my grasp. The only thing closer to my hands than my bedsheets is a slice of cold pizza. I just want to eat in peace, thank you very much. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It is not unusual to go 48 hours with little sleep’: what it’s like to cover a Cop climate summit
articles.description: The UN’s annual climate conference began in Turkey this week. Reporting from the event can be gruelling work – but it’s also crucial. They are counting on you not to read our coverage of the Cop31 climate talks. Fossil fuel companies, climate science deniers, petrostates, far right populists … They want you to think the negotiations are too intractable, the progress too halting, the issues too complex, too tortuous, too pointless, TL;DR. But as the UN’s 31st annual climate conference got underway in Antalya, Turkey this week, our journalists have been going to great lengths to help you understand why the talks remain urgent , crucial and – hopefully – consequential. As well as helping you follow the agreements reached and progress made during the two week summit, they have also been highlighting what’s at stake . Continue reading...

articles.title: Spark review – Glyndebourne Youth Opera light up a terrific new show of monsters and magic
articles.description: Glyndebourne, Lewes Lucy Armstrong’s family opera transports audiences to a secret world above the rooftops. It explores themes of grief and loss with a lightness of touch, and is directed, designed and performed with panache. For decades now, Glyndebourne has been setting the bar for what a youth opera company can be. Its latest show is Spark, a new full-length opera directed by Fiona Dunn with music by Lucy Armstrong, exploring grownup themes of grief and loss. Spark is a story of a parallel world accessed via something unlikely, so there are shades of Narnia or Wonderland. Our heroine is Clara (shades of The Nutcracker), who has panic attacks when she tries to go to school: “They talk like it’s simple,” she says in Olivia Bell’s succinct, fluent libretto, “but my chest is tightening and I can’t breathe.” We find out that her anxiety stems from her grief for her brother, and that she can no longer connect with her parents, who are having connection problems of their own. But she can escape up the chimney to a rooftop land populated by Spark Monsters – who will help her regain her lost spark, pun intended. Continue reading...

articles.title: Tamsin Greig is sensational in a Cranford where comedy and pain are in perfect balance
articles.description: Orange Tree theatre, London This streamlined adaptation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel gets right to the heart of her characters, who face heartbreak and loss but gain from the strength of female friendship There’s more than one worry for any new dramatisation of Elizabeth Gaskell’s novel to contend with. There is the risk of this story, set among the unmarried women and widows of a fictional English town, being considered Middlemarch lite – and overshadowed by the Royal Shakespeare Company’s luminous adaptation of the George Eliot novel, currently running in Stratford-Upon-Avon . Then there is the 2007 BBC adaptation of Cranford, which threw every national treasure at it, trowelling on the loveable humour and sentiment as it did so. This production, however, co-created by Lin Coghlan, Shaun McKenna and Josh Roche, bypasses all those dangers by leaning into theatricality – and sheer good acting. The script is by Coghlan and McKenna, who previously adapted The Forsyte Saga, staged last year by the RSC. They confidently fillet the original and also add their own little inventions. articles.description: Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu , a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”. articles.title: The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial
articles.description: Renewed commitments to electrification and climate science are vital outcomes from the latest round of UN talks The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34. While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. articles.title: The Guardian view on civil service reform: AI cannot conjure a capable state on its own | Editorial
articles.description: Whitehall needs to change, but more technology isn’t enough. Opening routes to leadership would bring skills that are too often overlooked The cabinet secretary, Antonia Romeo, called for an overhaul of a “ reactive and risk-averse ” civil service in her speech last Tuesday. Ministers planned a “radical shift” of powers, resources and accountability to regional and local government, which she said would leave Whitehall “leaner and more strategic”. As 80% of civil servants already work outside London, devolution promises to alter what central government does, not simply where it operates. Reinvention is in the civil service’s blood – ever since it was founded as a permanent, impartial institution in 1854. Even departmental boundaries, Dame Antonia said, are on notice, asking  do they “remain optimal in an era of cross‑cutting delivery?” This must be set against the civil service’s relative decline: it is ranked joint sixth internationally on one measure of public administration. To improve, Dame Antonia says the civil service must embrace AI. The efficacy of public service, she claimed, no longer has to be constrained by the limits of “ human bandwidth ”. articles.description: Paul English says the cheap home charging that makes EVs economical is out of reach for many, while Mike Hawes wonders if consumers are ready to switch. Plus letters from Ben Plowden and Anne Maclennan George Monbiot is right that European carmakers have dragged their feet, but his column describes only half the problem ( Why are Britain’s streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them, 11 November ). About 40% of UK households have no off-street parking, rising to around 60% in urban areas. For us, the cheap home charging that makes electric vehicles (EVs) economical is out of reach. Ministers may have removed the need for planning permission for cross-pavement charging channels, yet more than 20 councils still refuse them , while others, like my own Green-run council, dither and leave residents waiting for a policy. articles.title: The ecological value of reintroducing white-tailed eagles to Britain | Letters
articles.description: Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley respond to concerns that the eagles would destroy seabird populations Your article ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) raises important questions, but overlooks a fundamental point: eagles and seabirds coexisted around Britain’s coastline for thousands of years before eagles were driven to extinction through human persecution. Predation and disturbance are therefore not novel ecological pressures, but historically established interactions that have been absent from much of the British landscape for over a century. There is a danger here of accepting an ecologically impoverished landscape as our conservation baseline. Seabird colonies have existed in the absence of a native apex predator, but that does not necessarily make predator-free conditions either natural or desirable. Restoring eagles is not simply about recovering a charismatic species; it is about restoring lost ecological relationships and processes. Continue reading...

articles.description: Andreeva seals 7-5, 6-3 victory to earn world No 2 ranking Russian dominates tournament without losing a set Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. Serving for the first set at 5-4, Andreeva nervously opened the game with two dire double faults before spraying two further unforced errors to hand over the break. There have already been many times in Andreeva’s young career when similar sequences triggered epic, dramatic collapses, so prone the 19-year-old has been to losing her composure when things do not go her way. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. Andreeva immediately retrieved the break and regained her momentum as she marched to a monumental victory, defeating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at Indian Wells for the first time. articles.title: ‘A songbook for protest movements’: how did this secret mission to smuggle antifascist music out of Spain ever get forgotten?
articles.description: In 1961, a group of Italian creatives crossed the border to collect anti-Franco resistance songs and share them with the world – sparking intense backlash from the dictator. A new documentary retraces that perilous journey In the summer of 1961, four Italians crossed the Pyrenees into fascist Spain. Unknown to the border guards, their car was loaded with microfilm, a tape recorder and, tucked in the pocket of a writer and musician named Sergio Liberovici, a book of matches – each split in half, etched with the addresses of Spanish antifascists in miniature and glued back together, a hairline fracture concealing secrets that, if discovered, could result in jail or worse. Along with Michele Luciano Straniero, Emilio Jona and Margherita Galante Garrone, Liberovici was a member of a leftwing collective named Cantacronache. Formed in 1958 and counting Italo Calvino and Umberto Eco among their collaborators, the collective was repulsed by the superficiality of Italian pop music and hoped to revitalise culture with Brechtian realism. articles.title: Accidents, emotional affairs and impromptu Leonard Cohen dancing - My Wife Cries review
articles.description: Angela Schanelec’s famously uncompromising work takes on a new warmth in this sometimes playful study of everyday emotional turmoil The elliptical cinema of German film-maker Angela Schanelec is often described as uncompromising. This latest work, however, radiates a striking warmth. We see a marriage tearing at the seams, but this untethering is devoid of the usual dramatic flourishes. On an ordinary day like any another, construction worker Thomas (Vladimir Vulevic) notices a missed call from his wife, Carla (Agathe Bonitzer); when he phones back, she doesn’t pick up. The event holds little significance for the mild-mannered man; he carries on his usual chitchat with his co-workers, mundane catchups that unfold over static, tableaux-like shots. This deceptive calm is ruptured, however, when Thomas finds Carla sobbing helplessly on a park bench. A seismic change has taken hold within her: she will later confide in him of an emotional affair, and a tragic accident that leaves her emotionally unmoored. articles.title: Migrants targeted, charity workers menaced for helping them. Are we that kind of society? | Natasha Walter
articles.description: I’ve seen how a new wave of hatred has changed the way the sector goes about its work, and now a report details this crisis. It must be a wake-up call Natasha Walter is the founder of Women for Refugee Women There is a small charity that brings its local community together every day in a centre made bright with flowers grown in its own little garden. People, old and young, migrant and citizen, eat meals together made from food that would otherwise go to waste. The children play with donated toys, the grownups learn English together. Last summer, they had an outing to the seaside and posted some of the joyful pictures online. They won’t do that again. Natasha Walter is an author and honorary professor at Queen Mary University of London. She is the founder of Women for Refugee Women Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Brock Purdy was once dismissed as a system guy. Now he is THE guy
articles.description: The San Francisco 49ers quarterback was long seen as the beneficiary of the tools at his disposal. This season, he’s setting fire to that narrative The Cowboys entered this week having given up the second-most points in the NFC, but there was a particular elegance to the beating Brock Purdy put on them as the 49ers moved to 8-1 with a 46-40 shootout win in front of a sullen Jerry Jones in north Texas. Purdy has presided over lots of routs since he took over the offense in 2022, but this particular defeat of the Cowboys had a unique feel to it. Purdy, who is often dismissed as benefiting from a hospitable 49ers system, was a wrecking crew. That was true in the statistical sense, as Purdy closed with 389 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-28 passing. Later in the game, it became true in the literal sense as Purdy ended one of his greatest games in style. Continue reading...

articles.title: Leihani Zoric, 14, stuns surfing world with gold medal to give Australia Olympic boost
articles.description: Teenager’s ISA World Surfing Games win earns extra place at LA Games Compatriot Ethan Ewing also wins gold at men’s event in Peru Australian surfing prodigy Leihani Zoric’s meteoric rise appears to have no bounds after the 14-year-old upstaged a star-studded field at the ISA World Surfing Games to claim individual gold and earn her team a crucial boost ahead of the 2028 LA Olympics. Zoric, who only turned 14 earlier this month, became the youngest champion in the tournament’s history after getting the better of a wealth of more experienced surfers at the event in Peru. Continue reading...

articles.title: Special needs overhaul in England could bring in new avenues for extra support

The move comes as the government’s reforms are being repeatedly criticised by campaigners and parents’ groups for watering down legal protections allowing families to appeal through a high court tribunal for support. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches

Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say. Continue reading...

articles.title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told
articles.description: Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week. The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets. Continue reading...

articles.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
articles.description: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters
articles.description: Once ‘famine food’, empty granaries have forced people along the Shire River to harvest water-lily roots in waters full of the reptiles The mid-morning heat in Malawi’s lower Shire River basin is already suffocating, but Beatrice Maseko cannot afford to look away from the water’s edge. Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika . Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface. Continue reading...

articles.title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
articles.description: Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. Continue reading...

articles.title: Midnight Diner: Netflix just dropped its most beautiful show in years … and it’s barely been noticed
articles.description: Disarmingly thoughtful stillness is the order of the day in the latest season of this Japanese show about a Tokyo eatery. What a shame it feels buried under other content The first time we see the Master (Kaoru Kobayashi) in the sixth season of Midnight Diner, he cuts a curiously morose figure. His usually bustling establishment – open from midnight to 7am – is empty. No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. An ironic start for a drama arriving after a seven-year absence, delayed in part by uncertainty over the pandemic’s impact on small eateries. The show’s return isn’t a shock. Based on Yarō Abe’s long-running manga, it has been a TV fixture in Japan since 2009. Netflix has just quietly released it, buried by the platform’s seeming aversion to marketing non-English series, which has swallowed reams of remarkable Japanese television. Continue reading...

articles.title: AIPAC dumped more than $55 million into losing midterm races
articles.description: The largest pro-Israel group in the U.S., the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has been silent on social media since Tuesday afternoon, well before polls closed across the country and Democrats won both chambers of Congress in a blue wave, largely driven by dissatisfaction over rising costs sparked by the war in Iran. The group was an early supporter of the war and a major funder of ads attacking House and Senate candidates calling to cut off aid to Israel. It spent big on the 2026 midterm elections, dumping $84.1 million via its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), and several other PACs into races that have been decided as of this writing. AIPAC might be silent today because they need to explain to their donors how nearly-two-thirds, or $55.3 million, of that spending went to races in which the group’s preferred candidate lost. A failure to achieve the desired results from two-thirds of its political spending will be a tough reality to present to donors, especially when AIPAC repeatedly claims that “being pro-Israel is good policy and good politics.” AIPAC’s failures to deliver results for its donors stands in sharp contrast with the 2022 midterm election,

articles.title: Vance admits it: ‘The reason we lost is the war’
articles.description: Wednesday morning, as Democrats celebrated one of the largest midterm blowouts in decades, Vice President J.D. Vance struck a somber tone. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X, referencing the Iran conflict the Trump administration launched in February of this year. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he continued. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” While Vance has long hinted at skepticism toward the Iran war, the comments represent an unusually clear criticism by a vice president of his own president’s policy. The statement suggests Vance sees a need to distance himself from the conflict in hopes of bolstering his future political fortunes, particularly ahead of a likely run for president in 2028. President Donald Trump acknowledged Tuesday that Iran “was a piece of it” but insisted that he “did the right thing. I would have done it again.” Indeed, there is little doubt that the Iran war played a decisive role in the Democrats’ dominant performance on Tuesday. articles.title: Major losses could spur Trump to escalate war before year's end
articles.description: As much as the Iran war is the key reason Trump and the GOP were crushed tonight, it is important to recognize that the pressure for war is now likely to increase . This does not mean that Trump will restart the war. But the balance of pressure for and against war will likely favor escalation. Trump was under a degree of pressure to strike a deal before the midterms, hoping to soften the blow in the polls. But now that the midterms are over, that pressure will dissipate somewhat. Gas prices are still high, but the political cost has already been paid. There won’t be another point on the political calendar for some time when that cost can be exacted again. But two other factors will intensify. First, pro-war elements in Israel and in Washington will see the next two months as the last period in which Trump has wide maneuverability to restart the war. By January, the Democrats will control both chambers, will control the purse, and can begin impeaching Trump’s secretaries, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
